Good afternoon, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. We are gathered here today to finalize the work we have performed on Committee I during the 15th United Nations Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, and our work has been substantial and wide-ranging. We have conducted two interesting workshops. We can all be proud of the work and the efforts that we have jointly undertaken to accomplish these tasks. We have the workshop on building resilient societies with a focus on protecting women, children and youth, fostering engagement, education and the culture of lawfulness. During this workshop, participants emphasized the importance of preventive strategies that address the root causes of crime by strengthening protective factors at the individual, family, and community levels. Discussions highlighted the value of data, research, and evaluation in designing evidence-based interventions, while underscoring the need to move from consultations to co-creation by meaningfully involving women, children, young people, survivors and persons with lived experience in the development of crime prevention and criminal justice policies and programs. Participants also encouraged Member States to invest in community engagement and resilience building measures that promote social cohesion, trust in institutions and the culture of lawfulness in line with the Kyoto Declaration and the Abu Dhabi Declaration. We next turned our efforts to conducting a workshop on getting ahead, strengthening data collection and analysis to better protect people and planet in times of new, emerging and evolving forms of crime. In this workshop, participants emphasized that high quality, standardized, and interoperable data are essential for understanding and responding to new, emerging, and evolving forms of crime, including those that are increasingly transnational and technology enabled. They highlighted the importance of strengthening data management, implementing international statistical standards, enhancing international cooperation and data sharing, and making better use of both traditional and non-traditional data sources to support timely, evidence-based, and people-centered crime prevention and criminal justice responses. I'm proud and grateful for the substantive, concrete, fruitful work that we have accomplished. This work has been fully captured and summarized in a draft report of Committee 1. Our last efforts will now be devoted to the adoption of this report, which will then be presented for adoption by the plenary in the morning of Thursday, 1st of October.
